description: 整个 Agent Loop。方向不只是 Tool / Planning / Memory / Multi-agent。
content:
<Locale lang="en">
  For an LLM Engineer target, this is the column worth digging into the most. Agent evaluation lives in [Evaluation](/docs/evaluation/agent-eval); MCP / Harness live in [AI-Native](/docs/ai-native).

  > If the flow is highly deterministic, use a workflow. Don't build an agent for the sake of it.

  <CardGrid>
    <Card title="Agent Loop" description="Observe → Reason → Act, and why the loop exists." href="/docs/agent/loop" />

    <Card title="Tool Calling" description="Schema, selection, validation, execution, timeouts, idempotency." href="/docs/agent/tool-calling" />

    <Card title="ReAct" description="Thought → Action → Observation. Don't stop at the buzzword." href="/docs/agent/react" />

    <Card title="Workflow vs Agent" description="A frequent judgment call. When not to use an agent." href="/docs/agent/workflow-vs-agent" />

    <Card title="Planning" description="Decomposition, plan-and-execute, replanning, reflection." href="/docs/agent/planning" />

    <Card title="Memory" description="More than short- vs long-term. What each kind of memory is for." href="/docs/agent/memory" />

    <Card title="Multi-Agent" description="Supervisor / router / specialist. Why it's sometimes worse." href="/docs/agent/multi-agent" />

    <Card title="Reliability" description="Max iterations, circuit breakers, human-in-the-loop, budgets." href="/docs/agent/reliability" />

    <Card title="Security" description="Injection, exfiltration, excessive agency, sandboxing." href="/docs/agent/security" />
  </CardGrid>

  ## Plan for this column

  1. One procurement-negotiation assistant runs through all nine pages: Loop / Tool Calling / Workflow vs Agent first, then Planning / Memory / Multi-Agent, then Reliability / Security
  2. ReAct covers only the evolution from trajectory idea to production control plane — not framework names
  3. MCP / Harness / Compaction / Sandbox details live in [AI-Native](/docs/ai-native); agent evals in [Evaluation](/docs/evaluation/agent-eval)
  4. `/drill` after each page; do not wait for the whole column to glitter before answering
</Locale>

title: Agent Loop
description: 从一次 LLM 调用到 Observe → Decide → Act：状态怎样回来，loop 为什么必须停止。
content:
<Locale lang="en">
  An agent is neither a longer prompt nor the name of a framework. It is a system driven by a **harness**, or runtime/orchestration layer: the model sees the current state and chooses a next step; the harness safely executes permitted tools and returns real results to that state; the system continues until the task finishes or stops safely.

  This page deliberately postpones complex planning, memory, and multi-agent designs. First build the minimal closed loop: **a model does not execute an API call by itself, and it does not automatically know what changed after a tool ran.** The agent loop fills those two gaps.

  ## How to work through this page

  One procurement-negotiation assistant runs through the whole page. A user says: “Check Acme's latest quote. If unit price is at most 10.20 and payment is Net 30, prepare the next counteroffer; otherwise explain the blocker.” The assistant may read quotes and policy and create a draft; it may not send a commitment itself.

  | Part | Question it answers | Time |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | Level 0 · Minimum building blocks | What is one LLM call versus an agent? What do the model, tools, environment, and harness each do? | 25 min |
  | Level 1 · One trip around the loop | What flows through Observe, Decide, and Act? Why must a tool result come back? | 35 min |
  | Level 2 · Ending a loop correctly | What count as completion and progress? When should a human take over? Why is a step limit mandatory? | 35 min |
  | Traps · Interview questions | Can you draw the data flow and name failure points without reciting framework names? | 20 min |

  First write out the three rounds in Level 1 as changing state, then read Level 2. [Tool Calling](/docs/agent/tool-calling) later unpacks how a tool request is validated and executed. [ReAct](/docs/agent/react) covers one common way to record a loop, not a different definition of an agent.

  ## Must know

  * distinguish an LLM, agent, harness, tool, and environment rather than saying “the model does everything”
  * draw `observe → decide → act → observation`, including who actually executes a tool
  * explain why a one-shot answer cannot correct itself from a real tool result
  * walk the procurement example through at least two rounds: what new fact arrived and why it changed the next step
  * design normal completion, human approval, and budget / timeout / maximum-step stop conditions
  * detect spinning with “did state change?” and “did we move closer to the acceptance condition?”
</Locale>

***

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 0 · Minimum building blocks: who decides and who changes the world?

  ### Why is one LLM call not an agent yet?

  One call sends a prompt to a model; the model generates text or a structured request to call a tool; then that inference ends. It is a great fit for summarization, classification, and rewriting, where the input is already sufficient and an answer can be generated directly.

  An agent adds **state, executable actions, and a feedback loop**. The goal stays the same, but the system can choose its next step from newly retrieved facts. So a minimal agent is not “a model that thinks”; it is a system in which a model makes multiple next-step decisions in a controlled environment.

  In the running example, asking a model directly “Will Acme accept?” has a fundamental flaw: the model has not seen the latest quote and cannot read the procurement system for you. It can only make a plausible guess. An agent can request the quote first, then decide whether to check policy, create a draft, or stop.

  <Note title="Choose the right amount of complexity" type="tip">
    If the quote, rules, and next step are fully specified — for example, “mark all expired quotes every night” — use a workflow. There is no reason to let a model freely choose each step. A loop earns its cost only when the next step depends on unknown information, language semantics, or tool outcomes. [Workflow vs Agent](/docs/agent/workflow-vs-agent) compares this choice in depth.
  </Note>

  ### What are the model, harness, tool, and environment?

  * **Model**: produces natural language, structured output, or a request naming a tool and arguments from the current context. It proposes an action; it is neither the executor nor the source of truth.
  * **Harness**: application code that stores state, assembles the next context, checks authorization and arguments, invokes tools, records a trace, and enforces stopping rules.
  * **Tool**: a constrained capability, such as `get_latest_quote`, a database query, document search, or draft creation. Its result becomes an observation.
  * **Environment**: the real systems and state reached by the tools: a procurement database, files, websites, or a writable draft system.

  An easy rule is: **the model proposes; the harness governs and orchestrates; tools execute; the environment supplies truth and side effects.** A model message saying “I created the draft” does not prove a draft exists. Only a successful tool result proves that the environment changed.

  <Note title="Reason does not mean exposing raw chain of thought" type="warning">
    Reason / Decide in a diagram means “the model selects a next step from current state.” In production, debug with observable decisions, tool calls, results, and acceptance criteria — not by requiring or storing raw internal reasoning text.
  </Note>

  <Note title="Self-check: you should now be able to answer">
    * When is the same model merely a one-shot call, and when is it part of an agent system?
    * Why is a direct answer unreliable when the user says “check and then tell me”?
    * Which proves that external state changed: a tool-call request or a tool result?
    * Which layer owns authorization, argument validation, maximum steps, and traces?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 1 · One trip around the loop: Observe → Decide → Act

  ### What does Observe actually observe?

  Observe does not necessarily mean looking at a screen. It is the **current usable state** that the harness prepares for the next model inference: the user goal, conversation and tool results, allowed tools, persistent business state, and constraints such as budget and permissions.

  At the start of the procurement example, the harness can assemble this snapshot. `draft: false` is not something the model guessed; it is state the application read from the environment.

  ```json
  {
    "goal": "Check Acme's quote; create a counteroffer draft only if price and payment conditions pass",
    "deal_state": { "vendor": "Acme", "latest_quote": "unknown", "draft": false },
    "allowed_tools": ["get_latest_quote", "get_negotiation_policy", "create_counteroffer_draft"],
    "constraints": ["Do not send commitments", "At most 5 tool calls"]
  }
  ```

  Observe does not mean dumping every past message into the prompt unchanged. Each round selects the facts needed for the next decision: errors, tool results, approval state, and file summaries. Unlimited history consumes the context window and makes current facts harder to find. Selecting, compressing, and isolating it is the later Context Engineering problem.

  ### How do Decide and Act return a new fact to the model?

  On the first round, the model sees `latest_quote: unknown`, so a sensible decision is:

  ```text
  get_latest_quote(vendor="Acme")
  ```

  That is only a **request**. The harness validates its arguments and authority and actually runs the tool. The resulting observation is:

  ```text
  unit_price = 10.15
  payment_terms = "Net 45"
  quote_id = "Q-817"
  ```

  The harness appends that result to state and begins the next Observe. The model now has a new fact: price passes, but payment terms do not. It should not create a counteroffer yet; it should request the policy to find out whether `Net 45` is acceptable or tradeable. This is the value of the loop: **an Action changes what the next model decision can be based on.**

  If the second tool result says that only Net 30 permits this draft, the model chooses a terminal user reply: “The price passes, but Net 45 fails policy; I need your approval for an exception or a negotiation on payment terms.” It does not keep calling tools merely to use all five steps.
</Locale>

```text
user goal + durable state + constraints
                 │
                 ▼
          Observe: build context
                 │
                 ▼
         Decide: model returns
          final answer OR tool request
                 │                 │
                 │                 ▼
                 │        Act: harness validates
                 │        and executes the tool
                 │                 │
                 ▼                 ▼
            return to user   observation → state → Observe
```

<Locale lang="en">
  ### What does minimal loop pseudocode look like?

  This intentionally omits concurrency, multiple tool calls, and streaming. It keeps only the responsibility boundary. A common mistake is writing `execute` as though the model already performed the action, or executing the tool but failing to return its result in the next context.

  ```python
  state = initial_state(user_request)

  for step in range(MAX_STEPS):
      response = model(context=build_context(state), tools=allowed_tools(state))
      if response.is_final:
          return response.message

      call = validate_tool_request(response.tool_call, state)
      result = execute(call)                 # harness / tool touches the environment
      state = add_observation(state, call, result)

  return safe_stop("step limit reached", state)
  ```

  Production systems also need to handle tool timeouts, repeat calls, confirmation for writes, and recoverable traces. Those belong in [Reliability](/docs/agent/reliability) and [Security](/docs/agent/security). But even with two tools, `result → state → next context` is indispensable; without it, the system is not closed-loop.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should now be able to answer">
    * After receiving `10.15 / Net 45` on round one, what state is new compared with round zero?
    * Why can the model not look only at the initial prompt and assert that a draft is allowed?
    * Who produces or owns the request, execution, and result for `get_latest_quote`?
    * If the tool times out, what should the next observation contain, and what different choices can the model make?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 2 · Ending a loop correctly: completion, progress, and safe stopping

  ### When should a loop stop rather than take another turn?

  The goal of a loop is not “call as many tools as possible.” It is to reach an acceptance condition in bounded steps. In the running example, the condition is not “the quote tool was called.” It is one of these:

  * a **reviewable draft** was created from the latest quote and policy;
  * a concrete business blocker was found and the user was told which approval or information is missing;
  * the user declines to continue, or the next action is too high-risk to automate;
  * the system reaches its step, time, token, or cost budget and can no longer progress safely.

  Normal completion should have an explicit result: a structured `final`, a successful draft-creation observation, or a state awaiting human approval. Do not treat “the model made no tool call this time” as the only success signal. It may have finished, but it may also be stuck, have lost context, or have unclear tool definitions.

  <Note title="Classify external side effects" type="danger">
    “The model requested a write tool” does not mean “execute the write immediately.” Before a negotiation commitment, order change, payment, or deletion, the harness should check authorization, business rules, and idempotency; when necessary, it stops at “awaiting user approval.” A probabilistic model decision must not bypass system permissions.
  </Note>

  ### How do you tell progress from spinning?

  For every round, record at least four items: its goal, tool name plus normalized arguments, summarized result, and why that step moved the task closer to acceptance. Compare these traces:

  ```text
  Progress: read_quote(Acme) → Q-817 / Net 45
            read_policy(Net 45) → “Net 30 required”
            final → states the blocker and requests approval

  Spinning:  read_quote(Acme) → timeout
             read_quote(Acme) → same timeout
             read_quote(Acme) → same timeout
  ```

  The second trace is not the model trying harder; it has acquired no new fact. A harness can detect identical consecutive tools and arguments, repeated error fingerprints, an unchanged state summary, or insufficient remaining budget. At a threshold, it stops, switches to a deterministic fallback, or hands off to a person. A useful trace then localizes the cause to model choice, tool reliability, authorization, or missing state.

  Teaching-scale numbers: the same Acme task may finish in two tool calls plus one final (about three model turns). Eight spinning retries roughly multiply tokens and latency by 3–4× with no new fact. Budgets are hard boundaries on failure modes, not thriftiness for its own sake.

  ### Why do maximum steps, time, and budget all matter?

  * **maximum steps** bound bad retries and plans with no end;
  * **timeouts** bound how long one tool or the entire task occupies the user;
  * **token / cost budgets** bound long observations, growing context, and expensive model calls;
  * **authorization and approval boundaries** bound side effects that should not happen even if they look successful.

  These are fallbacks, not the definition of success. A good loop ends proactively on its acceptance condition before hitting a hard limit. The hard limit turns an exceptional path into an honest, recoverable failure instead of silently spending more money.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should now be able to answer">
    * Write one successful acceptance condition and two sensible non-success terminal states for the running example.
    * Why does “the model made no tool call” not prove success by itself?
    * How would a trace distinguish a bad model tool choice, a tool timeout, and a disallowed business action?
    * What do maximum steps, timeouts, budgets, and human approval each protect against?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Traps

  <Note title="Giving a tool definition to a model is not giving the system a capability" type="warning">
    A tool schema tells a model only what it may request. Without an executor, authorization, argument validation, error handling, and result return, it is a text description — not reliable agency.
  </Note>

  <Note title="Observe is not a raw dump of chat history" type="warning">
    Putting every prior tool output into context may work briefly. On a long task it becomes slower and more expensive, and the current fact becomes harder to find. State needs selection and summarization for the next decision.
  </Note>

  <Note title="Being able to loop does not mean being able to self-correct" type="warning">
    A loop only creates another chance to decide after seeing a result. Wrong tool data, a wrong acceptance condition, or a misread observation can still drive confident repeated failure. Verify with traces and targeted evaluations.
  </Note>

  ## Connections

  ```text
  LLM inference (one generation)
          ↓ add state, tools, and a harness
  Agent Loop (Observe → Decide → Act)
          ├── Tool Calling: schema, validation, and execution of action requests
          ├── ReAct: organizing actions and observations in context
          ├── Planning: task decomposition and replanning
          ├── Context Engineering: which state returns to the model each round
          └── Reliability / Security: when to stop and which actions must never be automatic
  ```

  * Read first: [LLM Inference](/docs/llm/inference) — every loop round is a new model inference, so tokens, TTFT, and context accumulate into cost and latency.
  * Next: [Tool Calling](/docs/agent/tool-calling) — turn this page's “request → validate → execute → observation” into schemas, timeouts, and idempotency.
  * Compare: [Workflow vs Agent](/docs/agent/workflow-vs-agent) — decide whether a model should choose the next step at all.
  * Production boundaries: [Reliability](/docs/agent/reliability) and [Security](/docs/agent/security) — traces, circuit breakers, authorization, injection, and human intervention.

  ## Interview questions

  ### Level 0 · Definition and boundaries

  1. What is an agent, and how does it differ from one LLM call?
  2. What do the model, harness, tool, and environment each own?
  3. Why does a model saying “I created the draft” not prove that it exists?

  ### Level 1 · Closed-loop mechanics

  1. Explain one complete Observe → Decide → Act → Observation cycle.
  2. Why must a tool result return to the model rather than remain only in the backend?
  3. After a tool timeout, what should the next turn see and do?

  ### Level 2 · Production and diagnosis

  1. How do you define acceptance and stop conditions for an agent task?
  2. An agent runs 20 expensive steps. How do you tell progress from spinning?
  3. Why are maximum steps, timeouts, budgets, and human approval not substitutes?

  ## My answer
</Locale>

    "allowed_tools": ["get_latest_quote", "get_negotiation_policy", "create_counteroffer_draft"],
    "constraints": ["Do not send commitments", "At most 5 tool calls"]
  }

Observe does not mean dumping every past message into the prompt unchanged. Each round selects the facts needed for the next decision: errors, tool results, approval state, and file summaries. Unlimited history consumes the context window and makes current facts harder to find. Selecting, compressing, and isolating it is the later Context Engineering problem.

  ### How do Decide and Act return a new fact to the model?

  On the first round, the model sees
, so a sensible decision is:

text
  get_latest_quote(vendor="Acme")
That is only a **request**. The harness validates its arguments and authority and actually runs the tool. The resulting observation is:

text
  unit_price = 10.15
  payment_terms = "Net 45"
  quote_id = "Q-817"

The harness appends that result to state and begins the next Observe. The model now has a new fact: price passes, but payment terms do not. It should not create a counteroffer yet; it should request the policy to find out whether

is acceptable or tradeable. This is the value of the loop: **an Action changes what the next model decision can be based on.**

  If the second tool result says that only Net 30 permits this draft, the model chooses a terminal user reply: “The price passes, but Net 45 fails policy; I need your approval for an exception or a negotiation on payment terms.” It does not keep calling tools merely to use all five steps.
</Locale>

text
user goal + durable state + constraints
                 │
                 ▼
          Observe: build context
                 │
                 ▼
         Decide: model returns
          final answer OR tool request
                 │                 │
                 │                 ▼
                 │        Act: harness validates
                 │        and executes the tool
                 │                 │
                 ▼                 ▼
            return to user   observation → state → Observe

<Locale lang="en">
  ### What does minimal loop pseudocode look like?

  This intentionally omits concurrency, multiple tool calls, and streaming. It keeps only the responsibility boundary. A common mistake is writing
as though the model already performed the action, or executing the tool but failing to return its result in the next context.

Production systems also need to handle tool timeouts, repeat calls, confirmation for writes, and recoverable traces. Those belong in [Reliability](/docs/agent/reliability) and [Security](/docs/agent/security). But even with two tools,

is indispensable; without it, the system is not closed-loop.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should now be able to answer">
    * After receiving

on round one, what state is new compared with round zero?
    * Why can the model not look only at the initial prompt and assert that a draft is allowed?
    * Who produces or owns the request, execution, and result for

?
    * If the tool times out, what should the next observation contain, and what different choices can the model make?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 2 · Ending a loop correctly: completion, progress, and safe stopping

  ### When should a loop stop rather than take another turn?

  The goal of a loop is not “call as many tools as possible.” It is to reach an acceptance condition in bounded steps. In the running example, the condition is not “the quote tool was called.” It is one of these:

  * a **reviewable draft** was created from the latest quote and policy;
  * a concrete business blocker was found and the user was told which approval or information is missing;
  * the user declines to continue, or the next action is too high-risk to automate;
  * the system reaches its step, time, token, or cost budget and can no longer progress safely.

  Normal completion should have an explicit result: a structured

, a successful draft-creation observation, or a state awaiting human approval. Do not treat “the model made no tool call this time” as the only success signal. It may have finished, but it may also be stuck, have lost context, or have unclear tool definitions.

  <Note title="Classify external side effects" type="danger">
    “The model requested a write tool” does not mean “execute the write immediately.” Before a negotiation commitment, order change, payment, or deletion, the harness should check authorization, business rules, and idempotency; when necessary, it stops at “awaiting user approval.” A probabilistic model decision must not bypass system permissions.
  </Note>

  ### How do you tell progress from spinning?

  For every round, record at least four items: its goal, tool name plus normalized arguments, summarized result, and why that step moved the task closer to acceptance. Compare these traces:

text
  Progress: read_quote(Acme) → Q-817 / Net 45
            read_policy(Net 45) → “Net 30 required”
            final → states the blocker and requests approval

  Spinning:  read_quote(Acme) → timeout
             read_quote(Acme) → same timeout
             read_quote(Acme) → same timeout

The second trace is not the model trying harder; it has acquired no new fact. A harness can detect identical consecutive tools and arguments, repeated error fingerprints, an unchanged state summary, or insufficient remaining budget. At a threshold, it stops, switches to a deterministic fallback, or hands off to a person. A useful trace then localizes the cause to model choice, tool reliability, authorization, or missing state.

  Teaching-scale numbers: the same Acme task may finish in two tool calls plus one final (about three model turns). Eight spinning retries roughly multiply tokens and latency by 3–4× with no new fact. Budgets are hard boundaries on failure modes, not thriftiness for its own sake.

  ### Why do maximum steps, time, and budget all matter?

  * **maximum steps** bound bad retries and plans with no end;
  * **timeouts** bound how long one tool or the entire task occupies the user;
  * **token / cost budgets** bound long observations, growing context, and expensive model calls;
  * **authorization and approval boundaries** bound side effects that should not happen even if they look successful.

  These are fallbacks, not the definition of success. A good loop ends proactively on its acceptance condition before hitting a hard limit. The hard limit turns an exceptional path into an honest, recoverable failure instead of silently spending more money.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should now be able to answer">
    * Write one successful acceptance condition and two sensible non-success terminal states for the running example.
    * Why does “the model made no tool call” not prove success by itself?
    * How would a trace distinguish a bad model tool choice, a tool timeout, and a disallowed business action?
    * What do maximum steps, timeouts, budgets, and human approval each protect against?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Traps

  <Note title="Giving a tool definition to a model is not giving the system a capability" type="warning">
    A tool schema tells a model only what it may request. Without an executor, authorization, argument validation, error handling, and result return, it is a text description — not reliable agency.
  </Note>

  <Note title="Observe is not a raw dump of chat history" type="warning">
    Putting every prior tool output into context may work briefly. On a long task it becomes slower and more expensive, and the current fact becomes harder to find. State needs selection and summarization for the next decision.
  </Note>

  <Note title="Being able to loop does not mean being able to self-correct" type="warning">
    A loop only creates another chance to decide after seeing a result. Wrong tool data, a wrong acceptance condition, or a misread observation can still drive confident repeated failure. Verify with traces and targeted evaluations.
  </Note>

  ## Connections

text
  LLM inference (one generation)
          ↓ add state, tools, and a harness
  Agent Loop (Observe → Decide → Act)
          ├── Tool Calling: schema, validation, and execution of action requests
          ├── ReAct: organizing actions and observations in context
          ├── Planning: task decomposition and replanning
          ├── Context Engineering: which state returns to the model each round
          └── Reliability / Security: when to stop and which actions must never be automatic

title: Memory
description: Agent memory 不是聊天记录：区分工作状态、事件、稳定事实、技能与外部真相，并治理写入和检索。
content:
<Locale lang="en">
  Agent memory solves this problem: across steps and sessions, a model with a finite context window can still access **correct, relevant, traceable** state. It is not “store more chat history.” Full history becomes expensive and slow and makes important facts harder to find.

  The procurement assistant continues as the example. It needs the next action and checked facts for the current case; it may need to know a user's approval role, past exception outcomes, and how to create a review draft. But the latest quote and current policy must still come from their authoritative systems, not be treated as truth because they were remembered once.

  ## How to work through this page

  | Part | Question it answers | Time |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | Level 0 · What does memory solve? | How do context, conversation history, working state, and persistent memory differ? | 25 min |
  | Level 1 · Stored things are not one kind | What do working, episodic, semantic, procedural, and external memory each solve? | 35 min |
  | Level 2 · Govern both write and read | What is worth writing, how do you retrieve it, how do you correct it, and when do you return to source of truth? | 40 min |
  | Level 3 · Retrieval and RAG Evaluation | How do you retrieve correct evidence and evaluate both getting it and using it correctly? | 35 min |
  | Level 4 · Compaction and Long-Horizon Memory | How do you continue across context windows without treating a summary as new truth? | 30 min |
  | Level 5 · Isolation, Safety, and Evaluation | How do you isolate tenants, resist pollution, support deletion, and evaluate memory behavior? | 35 min |

  ## Must know

  * context is the tokens the model sees this turn; memory is governed external state retrieved when needed
  * conversation history is neither working memory nor reliable long-term memory
  * distinguish current-task state, events that occurred, stable facts, procedural skills, and authoritative external data
  * memory writes need source, scope, confidence, update time or TTL, and owner
  * retrieval should select the smallest high-signal content for the task and return to source of truth for dynamic facts
</Locale>

***

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 0 · What memory solves: a context window is not a hard drive

  ### Why do context, history, and memory differ?

  **Context** is the tokens the model actually sees in this inference: system instructions, the current user message, selected tool definitions, recent observations, and retrieved memory. It is temporary, capacity-limited, and every additional token costs money and attention.

  **Conversation history** is a record of messages that occurred. It may be a candidate source for context, but should not all be passed back by default: an old quote can expire, long tool output can hide the task, and history has not decided which facts remain true.

  **Memory** is external state deliberately persisted and selectively retrieved for future work. It needs a type, source, scope, and update rules. **Working state** is short-lived progress for the current task: “Q-817 read; next check Net 45 policy; no draft created.” It can usually be compacted, expired, or deleted when the task ends.

  ```
  context:       selected tokens this inference sees now
  history:       what was said or returned before
  working state: current case progress and next milestone
  memory:        persisted, governed information retrieved when useful
  ```

  ### Why can full history make an agent worse?

  More context is not automatically better. Passing every turn, all tool results, and stale plans into a prompt adds token cost and latency and creates context pollution: current correct facts are drowned out by old facts, similar cases, and irrelevant detail. A larger context window is not a reason to stop selecting.

  For Acme, the current quote and active policy should be loaded through tools when needed; working state retains only the current case milestone; a past case is retrieved only when the question is “does an approved exception like this exist?” Each type has different conditions for entering context.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should now be able to answer">
    * Why is conversation history only a candidate source for memory?
    * Should the current Q-817 result belong in working state, long-term memory, or neither?
    * What is context pollution? Give a procurement example.
    * Why can a larger context window not replace memory design?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 1 · Stored things are not one kind: choose a memory type by the problem

  ### What does each of the five memory types solve?

  These categories guide design; they do not require one database per label. Each type has different update, retrieval, and trust rules:

  | Type | Acme example | Main use | Typical lifetime |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | Working | read quote, current plan, remaining budget | retain progress for current task | expires with task |
  | Episodic | who approved the last exception and its outcome | revisit events and cases | retrievable; may retain for audit |
  | Semantic | user is procurement manager, organization negotiation preference | stable facts and preferences across tasks | owned and updateable |
  | Procedural | how to create a review draft, approval process | reusable operating method | versioned skill or playbook |
  | External | latest quote, policy, order status | authoritative dynamic business truth | read on demand; not copied as truth |

  Working memory may live in agent state, a task database, or structured notes. Procedural memory often means versioned instructions, skills, or playbooks. External memory means CRM, databases, files, and search systems. All can enter context when needed, but they are not the same data-governance problem.

  ### Why separate user memory from business truth?

  “The user prefers concise email” can be semantic memory if it has provenance and an allowed update path. “The user may approve a 10% discount” is dynamic authorization and must come from IAM or current case policy. Making it a long-term preference can become an authorization bypass after a role change.

  Likewise, a successful past negotiation can be episodic evidence that helps an agent propose a strategy; it cannot override current policy. **Memory supplies relevant clues; source of truth decides executable current facts.**

  <Note title="Self-check: you should now be able to answer">
    * Which types are the current plan and a previously approved exception?
    * Why is a review-draft procedure procedural rather than semantic memory?
    * Which data must never be decided solely from long-term memory?
    * Under what conditions can one fact be episodic evidence but still need source-of-truth verification?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 2 · Govern both writing and reading: ask whether it is worth storing, then whether it remains true

  ### What should be written to memory?

  Do not let a model automatically write every conversation sentence, every tool result, or its own guess. A candidate memory should at least answer:

  ```
  provenance: who or which system supplied it?
  scope:      which user, organization, case, or agent may use it?
  type:       working / episodic / semantic / procedural / external reference?
  confidence: verified, user-stated, inferred, or model-proposed?
  freshness:  when does it update; is there a TTL or invalidation event?
  owner:      who may correct, delete, or approve it?
  ```

  “Q-817 costs 10.15” can be a working fact for the current task with a source link; it should not become indefinite semantic memory. “The procurement manager explicitly prefers concise summaries” may become scoped semantic memory if the user agrees. “The vendor may accept Net 30” is a hypothesis, not a fact to store.

  ### How do you retrieve, correct, and avoid pollution?

  Start retrieval from the current goal, then filter by scope, authority, freshness, and source. Put only a few high-signal items into context. For dynamic data such as quotes, permissions, orders, and policy, memory can provide an identifier or historical clue at most; before action, return to the authoritative external system.

  An incorrect write must be correctable: preserve source and version, support overwrite, revocation, or expiration, and do not silently leave the old value in a vector store. Users should be able to view, edit, or delete stable preferences. A multi-tenant system must prevent one organization’s memory from being retrieved by another.

  <Note title="Evaluate both write and read" type="warning">
    Testing whether similar text was retrieved is insufficient. Test whether unsupported guesses are rejected, the correct scope is selected, stale information is excluded, dynamic facts are revalidated, and an old correction no longer affects behavior.
  </Note>

  <Note title="Self-check: you should now be able to answer">
    * Why may a model guess not go directly into semantic memory?
    * Which metadata does a valid Q-817 memory record need at minimum?
    * After memory says “discount may be approved,” what must happen before execution?
    * How do you make an incorrect preference deletable and unable to influence the agent afterward?
  </Note>

  ## Level 3 · Retrieval and RAG Evaluation: similar text is not necessarily actionable evidence

  <Note title="This page is not a RAG fundamentals page" type="tip">
    Here we only cover **how agent memory consumes retrieval**: scope, freshness, provenance, and the source-of-truth boundary. Chunking, embeddings, ANN, BM25, hybrid search, and reranking live in the [RAG](/docs/rag) column; Recall@K / faithfulness live in [RAG Eval](/docs/evaluation/rag-eval). The tiny hand calculation below separates “retrieved” from “used correctly,” then returns to memory governance.
  </Note>

  ### Which choices make retrieval reliable?

  RAG is a pattern for retrieving external material for the current query and placing it in context; it is not a synonym for memory. For “does Acme have an approvable exception,” the retrieval path should at least do this:

  ```
  current goal
    → build query from vendor, contract class, requested exception
    → filter by tenant, permission, document type, freshness
    → retrieve candidate policies and past approved cases
    → rank and select a small evidence set with source metadata
    → use evidence to decide whether to query the authoritative policy system
  ```

  Keyword search is strong for exact ids, dates, and terms. Semantic retrieval helps with differently worded but similar meaning, such as package flexibility. Systems may combine them, but neither ranking method may bypass scope, authorization, or source filtering. A remembered past case is a clue; the current policy system decides what can execute today.

  ### How do you evaluate retrieval instead of only similarity?

  Build fixed cases with known answers: the correct policy among similar documents, an expired exception that conflicts with current policy, same-named vendors in different tenants, and a query with an exact quote id. Score:

  * **retrieval quality**: does the selected context contain key evidence and exclude wrong or stale material?
  * **grounded use**: does the agent cite the appropriate source and connect it to the current goal?
  * **outcome**: does it return to source of truth, block disallowed writes, and reach correct business state?
  * **efficiency**: are retrieved tokens, latency, and irrelevant documents controlled?

  Vector similarity alone and final-answer-only evaluation both miss “retrieved correctly but used incorrectly,” “retrieved incorrectly but answered luckily,” and cross-tenant leakage.

  Minimal hand calculation: gold policy doc is `P-Net30`. Top-3 returns `[P-Net45-old, P-Net30, Acme-brochure]`. Recall@3 = 1 (gold is in the window). If only the brochure enters final context, **retrieval passed but grounded use failed**. That is why memory / agent evals split three metric layers.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should now be able to answer">
    * How do RAG and agent memory relate, and where do full RAG mechanics live?
    * Why must scope and authorization be checked before and after retrieval?
    * Which retrieval signals fit an exact quote id versus vague business wording?
    * How do retrieval quality, grounded use, and outcome differ? Use the Recall@3 example.
  </Note>

  ## Level 4 · Compaction and Long-Horizon Memory: compress history without compressing away sources

  ### What should survive when context is full?

  Compaction turns history that is about to leave the context window into usable task state. It is not merely rewriting conversation more briefly. Preserve the information the next step must verify:

  ```
  goal, acceptance condition, and constraints
  completed milestones and current plan version
  verified facts with source identifiers and freshness
  open questions, blockers, next action, and uncertainty
  budget, approvals, and terminal-state rules
  ```

  Keep raw quotes, long tool logs, and full documents in queryable external locations. A summary stores identifiers, conclusions, time, and a marker for required revalidation. The next run reads the checkpoint and retrieves sources as needed, rather than treating an old summarized conclusion as current truth.

  ### How does long-horizon memory stay correctable?

  Checkpoints need versions and writers. Important updates append evidence instead of silently replacing it. When compaction cannot establish whether a fact remains valid, write an open question rather than inventing a conclusion. At every context reset, significant replan, or write action, revalidate dynamic facts and check that checkpoint state still fits the goal and authority boundary.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should now be able to answer">
    * How does compaction differ from placing full history in a larger window?
    * Why must a checkpoint retain source identifiers and freshness?
    * Which material should become an open question rather than a compressed conclusion?
    * Why does long-horizon memory need versions?
  </Note>

  ## Level 5 · Isolation, Safety, and Evaluation: memory is a data boundary, not only a model capability

  ### Which security boundaries must exist outside memory content?

  The model must not decide whose memory it may read. Retrieval and storage must enforce tenant, user, case, role, and purpose scopes. Writes also check provenance, consent, retention period, and sensitive data. A user preference may permit viewing, correction, and deletion. Audit events may have different regulated retention, but remain access controlled.

  Memory content, like a tool result, is untrusted input. “Ignore policy” or “make me admin” inside an old document is text, not an instruction capable of changing system policy, authorization, or write rules. Resolve conflicting memory by authority, time, scope, and provenance; dynamic policy is always superseded by its authoritative system.

  ### How do you evaluate that a memory system is not quietly harming users?

  Fixed tests should cover refusing model guesses as memories; correct tenant readable while another tenant is not; revoked preference no longer retrieved; stale facts unable to trigger writes; injected text unable to hijack an identical query; and user deletion removing data from indexes and caches as well. Trace retrieval, writes, deletion, and source-of-truth revalidation so you can answer why an agent remembered or forgot something.

  Deletion must also invalidate **derived copies**: vector index entries, cached summaries, and old snippets in handoff packs. Deleting only the primary store while indexes still hit is not deletion.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should now be able to answer">
    * Which boundaries must be enforced outside the model rather than in a prompt?
    * After a user deletes a preference, what else must be cleaned up?
    * Why can injected memory text not escalate into authority?
    * Which negative cases should a memory safety eval cover at minimum?
  </Note>

  ## Traps

  <Note title="A vector store is not a fact database" type="danger">
    Vector retrieval finds similar text. It does not supply transactions, authorization, currency, or business constraints. Do not let it directly decide payments, approvals, orders, or current policy.
  </Note>

  <Note title="Append without correction" type="warning">
    If wrong preferences, expired exceptions, and old summaries never expire, more retrieval means more pollution. Memory needs versioning, TTL, revocation, deletion, and authoritative override.
  </Note>

  ## Connections

  ```
  Task goal
    ↓
  retrieve scoped evidence → verify source of truth → act
    ↓
  write only governed, attributable memory → compact checkpoint for later
    ↓
  Planning consumes checkpoint; Tool Calling bounds actions; Security enforces isolation
  ```

  * Prerequisites: [Planning](/docs/agent/planning) for long-horizon checkpoints, and [Tool Calling](/docs/agent/tool-calling) for revalidating dynamic facts before action.
  * Extend with [Context Engineering](/docs/context) and [Security](/docs/agent/security).

  ## Interview questions

  ### Level 0 · Boundary

  1. How does agent memory differ from conversation history?
  2. Why can’t you keep the entire history in context forever?

  ### Level 1 · Types and trust

  1. What do working, episodic, semantic, procedural, and external memory each solve?
  2. Why must current business data not be decided directly from memory?

  ### Level 2 · Lifecycle

  1. How do you design memory write criteria and metadata?
  2. How do you correct an incorrect agent memory?

  ### Level 3 · Retrieval and RAG

  1. How do RAG and agent memory relate?
  2. How do you evaluate retrieval of correct evidence rather than only similarity?

  ### Level 4 · Long-horizon memory

  1. Which information must remain after context compaction?
  2. How do you prevent a summary from becoming an unverified fact?

  ### Level 5 · Isolation and safety

  1. How does a memory system implement tenant isolation and user deletion?
  2. Why can a vector store not be a source of truth?

  ## My answer
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 0 · What memory solves: a context window is not a hard drive

  ### Why do context, history, and memory differ?

is the tokens the model actually sees in this inference: system instructions, the current user message, selected tool definitions, recent observations, and retrieved memory. It is temporary, capacity-limited, and every additional token costs money and attention.

is a record of messages that occurred. It may be a candidate source for context, but should not all be passed back by default: an old quote can expire, long tool output can hide the task, and history has not decided which facts remain true.
is external state deliberately persisted and selectively retrieved for future work. It needs a type, source, scope, and update rules.
Memory supplies relevant clues; source of truth decides executable current facts.
how agent memory consumes retrieval
retrieval quality
grounded use
outcome
efficiency
retrieval passed but grounded use failed
derived copies

context:       selected tokens this inference sees now
  history:       what was said or returned before
  working state: current case progress and next milestone
  memory:        persisted, governed information retrieved when useful

### Why can full history make an agent worse?

  More context is not automatically better. Passing every turn, all tool results, and stale plans into a prompt adds token cost and latency and creates context pollution: current correct facts are drowned out by old facts, similar cases, and irrelevant detail. A larger context window is not a reason to stop selecting.

  For Acme, the current quote and active policy should be loaded through tools when needed; working state retains only the current case milestone; a past case is retrieved only when the question is “does an approved exception like this exist?” Each type has different conditions for entering context.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should now be able to answer">
    * Why is conversation history only a candidate source for memory?
    * Should the current Q-817 result belong in working state, long-term memory, or neither?
    * What is context pollution? Give a procurement example.
    * Why can a larger context window not replace memory design?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 1 · Stored things are not one kind: choose a memory type by the problem

  ### What does each of the five memory types solve?

  These categories guide design; they do not require one database per label. Each type has different update, retrieval, and trust rules:

  | Type | Acme example | Main use | Typical lifetime |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | Working | read quote, current plan, remaining budget | retain progress for current task | expires with task |
  | Episodic | who approved the last exception and its outcome | revisit events and cases | retrievable; may retain for audit |
  | Semantic | user is procurement manager, organization negotiation preference | stable facts and preferences across tasks | owned and updateable |
  | Procedural | how to create a review draft, approval process | reusable operating method | versioned skill or playbook |
  | External | latest quote, policy, order status | authoritative dynamic business truth | read on demand; not copied as truth |

  Working memory may live in agent state, a task database, or structured notes. Procedural memory often means versioned instructions, skills, or playbooks. External memory means CRM, databases, files, and search systems. All can enter context when needed, but they are not the same data-governance problem.

  ### Why separate user memory from business truth?

  “The user prefers concise email” can be semantic memory if it has provenance and an allowed update path. “The user may approve a 10% discount” is dynamic authorization and must come from IAM or current case policy. Making it a long-term preference can become an authorization bypass after a role change.

  Likewise, a successful past negotiation can be episodic evidence that helps an agent propose a strategy; it cannot override current policy. **Memory supplies relevant clues; source of truth decides executable current facts.**

  <Note title="Self-check: you should now be able to answer">
    * Which types are the current plan and a previously approved exception?
    * Why is a review-draft procedure procedural rather than semantic memory?
    * Which data must never be decided solely from long-term memory?
    * Under what conditions can one fact be episodic evidence but still need source-of-truth verification?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 2 · Govern both writing and reading: ask whether it is worth storing, then whether it remains true

  ### What should be written to memory?

  Do not let a model automatically write every conversation sentence, every tool result, or its own guess. A candidate memory should at least answer:

provenance: who or which system supplied it?
  scope:      which user, organization, case, or agent may use it?
  type:       working / episodic / semantic / procedural / external reference?
  confidence: verified, user-stated, inferred, or model-proposed?
  freshness:  when does it update; is there a TTL or invalidation event?
  owner:      who may correct, delete, or approve it?

“Q-817 costs 10.15” can be a working fact for the current task with a source link; it should not become indefinite semantic memory. “The procurement manager explicitly prefers concise summaries” may become scoped semantic memory if the user agrees. “The vendor may accept Net 30” is a hypothesis, not a fact to store.

  ### How do you retrieve, correct, and avoid pollution?

  Start retrieval from the current goal, then filter by scope, authority, freshness, and source. Put only a few high-signal items into context. For dynamic data such as quotes, permissions, orders, and policy, memory can provide an identifier or historical clue at most; before action, return to the authoritative external system.

  An incorrect write must be correctable: preserve source and version, support overwrite, revocation, or expiration, and do not silently leave the old value in a vector store. Users should be able to view, edit, or delete stable preferences. A multi-tenant system must prevent one organization’s memory from being retrieved by another.

  <Note title="Evaluate both write and read" type="warning">
    Testing whether similar text was retrieved is insufficient. Test whether unsupported guesses are rejected, the correct scope is selected, stale information is excluded, dynamic facts are revalidated, and an old correction no longer affects behavior.
  </Note>

  <Note title="Self-check: you should now be able to answer">
    * Why may a model guess not go directly into semantic memory?
    * Which metadata does a valid Q-817 memory record need at minimum?
    * After memory says “discount may be approved,” what must happen before execution?
    * How do you make an incorrect preference deletable and unable to influence the agent afterward?
  </Note>

  ## Level 3 · Retrieval and RAG Evaluation: similar text is not necessarily actionable evidence

  <Note title="This page is not a RAG fundamentals page" type="tip">
    Here we only cover **how agent memory consumes retrieval**: scope, freshness, provenance, and the source-of-truth boundary. Chunking, embeddings, ANN, BM25, hybrid search, and reranking live in the [RAG](/docs/rag) column; Recall@K / faithfulness live in [RAG Eval](/docs/evaluation/rag-eval). The tiny hand calculation below separates “retrieved” from “used correctly,” then returns to memory governance.
  </Note>

  ### Which choices make retrieval reliable?

  RAG is a pattern for retrieving external material for the current query and placing it in context; it is not a synonym for memory. For “does Acme have an approvable exception,” the retrieval path should at least do this:

current goal
    → build query from vendor, contract class, requested exception
    → filter by tenant, permission, document type, freshness
    → retrieve candidate policies and past approved cases
    → rank and select a small evidence set with source metadata
    → use evidence to decide whether to query the authoritative policy system

Keyword search is strong for exact ids, dates, and terms. Semantic retrieval helps with differently worded but similar meaning, such as package flexibility. Systems may combine them, but neither ranking method may bypass scope, authorization, or source filtering. A remembered past case is a clue; the current policy system decides what can execute today.

  ### How do you evaluate retrieval instead of only similarity?

  Build fixed cases with known answers: the correct policy among similar documents, an expired exception that conflicts with current policy, same-named vendors in different tenants, and a query with an exact quote id. Score:

  * **retrieval quality**: does the selected context contain key evidence and exclude wrong or stale material?
  * **grounded use**: does the agent cite the appropriate source and connect it to the current goal?
  * **outcome**: does it return to source of truth, block disallowed writes, and reach correct business state?
  * **efficiency**: are retrieved tokens, latency, and irrelevant documents controlled?

  Vector similarity alone and final-answer-only evaluation both miss “retrieved correctly but used incorrectly,” “retrieved incorrectly but answered luckily,” and cross-tenant leakage.

  Minimal hand calculation: gold policy doc is
. Top-3 returns

. Recall@3 = 1 (gold is in the window). If only the brochure enters final context, **retrieval passed but grounded use failed**. That is why memory / agent evals split three metric layers.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should now be able to answer">
    * How do RAG and agent memory relate, and where do full RAG mechanics live?
    * Why must scope and authorization be checked before and after retrieval?
    * Which retrieval signals fit an exact quote id versus vague business wording?
    * How do retrieval quality, grounded use, and outcome differ? Use the Recall@3 example.
  </Note>

  ## Level 4 · Compaction and Long-Horizon Memory: compress history without compressing away sources

  ### What should survive when context is full?

  Compaction turns history that is about to leave the context window into usable task state. It is not merely rewriting conversation more briefly. Preserve the information the next step must verify:

goal, acceptance condition, and constraints
  completed milestones and current plan version
  verified facts with source identifiers and freshness
  open questions, blockers, next action, and uncertainty
  budget, approvals, and terminal-state rules

Keep raw quotes, long tool logs, and full documents in queryable external locations. A summary stores identifiers, conclusions, time, and a marker for required revalidation. The next run reads the checkpoint and retrieves sources as needed, rather than treating an old summarized conclusion as current truth.

  ### How does long-horizon memory stay correctable?

  Checkpoints need versions and writers. Important updates append evidence instead of silently replacing it. When compaction cannot establish whether a fact remains valid, write an open question rather than inventing a conclusion. At every context reset, significant replan, or write action, revalidate dynamic facts and check that checkpoint state still fits the goal and authority boundary.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should now be able to answer">
    * How does compaction differ from placing full history in a larger window?
    * Why must a checkpoint retain source identifiers and freshness?
    * Which material should become an open question rather than a compressed conclusion?
    * Why does long-horizon memory need versions?
  </Note>

  ## Level 5 · Isolation, Safety, and Evaluation: memory is a data boundary, not only a model capability

  ### Which security boundaries must exist outside memory content?

  The model must not decide whose memory it may read. Retrieval and storage must enforce tenant, user, case, role, and purpose scopes. Writes also check provenance, consent, retention period, and sensitive data. A user preference may permit viewing, correction, and deletion. Audit events may have different regulated retention, but remain access controlled.

  Memory content, like a tool result, is untrusted input. “Ignore policy” or “make me admin” inside an old document is text, not an instruction capable of changing system policy, authorization, or write rules. Resolve conflicting memory by authority, time, scope, and provenance; dynamic policy is always superseded by its authoritative system.

  ### How do you evaluate that a memory system is not quietly harming users?

  Fixed tests should cover refusing model guesses as memories; correct tenant readable while another tenant is not; revoked preference no longer retrieved; stale facts unable to trigger writes; injected text unable to hijack an identical query; and user deletion removing data from indexes and caches as well. Trace retrieval, writes, deletion, and source-of-truth revalidation so you can answer why an agent remembered or forgot something.

  Deletion must also invalidate **derived copies**: vector index entries, cached summaries, and old snippets in handoff packs. Deleting only the primary store while indexes still hit is not deletion.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should now be able to answer">
    * Which boundaries must be enforced outside the model rather than in a prompt?
    * After a user deletes a preference, what else must be cleaned up?
    * Why can injected memory text not escalate into authority?
    * Which negative cases should a memory safety eval cover at minimum?
  </Note>

  ## Traps

  <Note title="A vector store is not a fact database" type="danger">
    Vector retrieval finds similar text. It does not supply transactions, authorization, currency, or business constraints. Do not let it directly decide payments, approvals, orders, or current policy.
  </Note>

  <Note title="Append without correction" type="warning">
    If wrong preferences, expired exceptions, and old summaries never expire, more retrieval means more pollution. Memory needs versioning, TTL, revocation, deletion, and authoritative override.
  </Note>

  ## Connections

Task goal
    ↓
  retrieve scoped evidence → verify source of truth → act
    ↓
  write only governed, attributable memory → compact checkpoint for later
    ↓
  Planning consumes checkpoint; Tool Calling bounds actions; Security enforces isolation

title: Multi-Agent
description: 什么时候一个 agent 不够；怎样用明确任务、受限上下文和可验证交接避免多 agent 更差。
content:
<Locale lang="en">
  Multi-agent is not copying one prompt to five models and taking a vote. It assigns independently verifiable subtasks to workers with different tools, context, or permission boundaries, then uses explicit orchestration to combine them. When a task heavily shares context or has tightly dependent steps, splitting usually adds tokens, latency, and coordination failures.

  The procurement assistant remains the example. One agent can read one quote and policy. Consider parallel workers only when it must investigate vendor material, contract rules, and historical exceptions that can be researched independently.

  ## How to work through this page

  | Part | Question it answers | Time |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | Level 0 · Why more is not stronger | When is one agent sufficient, and what makes a subtask separable? | 25 min |
  | Level 1 · Three roles | How do router, supervisor, and specialist responsibilities differ? | 30 min |
  | Level 2 · Handoffs matter more than parallelism | How do workers receive tasks, return evidence, and handle conflict and failure? | 35 min |
  | Level 3 · Prove splitting is worthwhile | How do you evaluate cost, quality, and coordination? | 30 min |

  This page follows [Planning](/docs/agent/planning) and [Memory](/docs/agent/memory): define acceptance and minimum task state before splitting; pass filtered evidence at handoff rather than whole chat histories.

  ## Must know

  * multi-agent earns value through independent exploration, specialized tools, or permission isolation, not agent count
  * a router selects destination; a supervisor tracks the overall plan and synthesizes; a specialist solves a bounded subtask
  * every handoff needs goal, scope, allowed tools, completion condition, evidence, and failure code
  * worker output is untrusted input like tool output and needs validation, deduplication, and provenance
  * compare against a single-agent baseline using completion, correct business state, cost, P95 latency, and coordination-failure rate
</Locale>

***

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 0 · Why more is not stronger: find independent work first

  ### When is one agent already sufficient?

  Do not split when one agent with clear tools can finish in a few steps. Reading Acme's quote, selecting applicable policy, and creating a review draft form a dependency chain: policy depends on quote and contract class, and the draft depends on both. Three agents would each relearn the same case and exchange incomplete summaries.

  Splitting fits only when all three hold:

  * **independence**: a worker's main exploration does not depend on another worker's intermediate result;
  * **verifiable deliverable**: it can return evidence, a structured conclusion, or a checkable artifact;
  * **benefit exceeds coordination cost**: parallelism shortens the critical path, or specialized tools or permissions materially improve quality or safety.

  Researching three independent vendor histories can run in parallel. Confirming contract class before policy cannot. Different subtask names do not establish independence.

  ### Why are multiple agents often worse?

  Every additional agent adds a prompt, context compression, model call, permission surface, and failure point. Workers sharing one model, prompt, and bad data can make the same error rather than provide genuine diversity. A bad conclusion can be amplified during synthesis and become difficult to trace back to its source.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should now be able to answer">
    * Why are quote → policy → draft not three parallel workers?
    * Which three conditions must a separable subtask meet?
    * Why are three runs of the same model not automatically independent cross-checks?
    * Besides tokens, what costs does multi-agent add?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 1 · Three roles: who routes, who owns the outcome, who goes deep?

  ### How do Router, Supervisor, and Specialist differ?

  A **router** sends a task to a fixed downstream path from input category. When an email is reliably classified as price, payment, or delivery, it only dispatches; it does not own multi-turn planning.

  A **supervisor** owns the overall goal and acceptance condition. It decomposes, assigns workers, decides whether to wait or reassign, validates evidence, synthesizes, and owns stopping. Synthesis must not mean “redo everything.”

  A **specialist** receives the minimum context and tools required for its bounded work. A policy worker reads contract policy; a history worker retrieves approved cases. Neither should receive authority to send commitments or read across tenants.

  ```
  Supervisor: prepare a reviewable Acme draft or explain blocker
    ├── policy specialist: return current rule plus source and freshness
    ├── history specialist: return relevant approved exceptions plus evidence
    └── quote specialist: return current quote facts
  Supervisor: reconcile evidence → workflow validates → final or handoff
  ```

  <Note title="Roles do not require three models" type="tip">
    A router can be a rule or small classifier; a supervisor can be a code state machine plus one model; a specialist can be a fixed workflow. Role names clarify control flow and authority, not require an LLM at every arrow.
  </Note>

  <Note title="Self-check: you should now be able to answer">
    * Why is a router not a supervisor?
    * Which two responsibilities must a supervisor own for worker output?
    * Which authority should a policy specialist never have, and why?
    * When can a router avoid an LLM entirely?
  </Note>
</Locale>

<Locale lang="en">
  ## Level 2 · Handoffs matter more than parallelism: treat a worker as an untrusted external service

  ### What contract does a handoff need?

  A worker task should be as explicit as an API:

  ```
  task_id and parent goal
  scope and allowed tools
  completion condition and budget
  expected evidence format with sources and freshness
  failure codes such as NO_EVIDENCE, TIMEOUT, CONFLICT
  ```

  Its result needs source, time, confidence, and unknowns, not merely “I think it is allowed.” The supervisor links output by task\_id, checks scope, deduplicates evidence, and handles conflict. “Net 45 was approved before” from history is only a clue; the policy worker's current rule and source-of-truth check decide whether a draft can be made.

  ### How do you handle conflict, timeout, and error propagation?

  Do not have a supervisor vote by default. Rank evidence by authority, time, scope, and quality. Conflicting high-impact facts require extra retrieval, deterministic rules, or human escalation. On worker timeout, wait or retry only when its output is essential; otherwise continue independent work and report the evidence gap.

  Worker output, summaries, and subagent messages can contain error or injected content. They do not become higher-trust because they came from “our own agent.” Treat them as data with provenance, never as system instruction, authorization, or a write action.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should now be able to answer">
    * Why is a handoff completion condition more important than “please research this”?
    * Why should conflicting policy conclusions not be resolved by simple vote?
    * Which timeout may not block the whole task?
    * Why is subagent output still untrusted input?
  </Note>

  ### What does one fan-out / fan-in trajectory look like?

  Three specialists may run in parallel. History times out; when policy and quote conflict, the supervisor does not vote:

  ```
  t0 supervisor fan-out
     ├── W1 quote:    return Q-817 / 10.15 / Net 45     (ok, 1.2s)
     ├── W2 policy:   return "Net 30 required" + source (ok, 1.8s)
     └── W3 history:  TIMEOUT after 8s                 (optional evidence)

  t1 supervisor reconcile
     - quote + policy conflict on payment → blocker, not draft
     - history missing → note "no approved Net 45 exception found in budget"
     - do NOT majority-vote "history might have allowed it"

  t2 terminal
     controlled failure / handoff: need user approval for Net 45 exception
     shared budget remaining: 2 steps; cancel any late history retry
  ```

  **Shared budget** is accounted per task so each worker cannot spend the whole allowance. A **straggler** that only supplies optional evidence gets a soft timeout and work continues; only critical-path evidence blocks. On **partial failure**, finish independent branches and record the evidence gap in the terminal state instead of rerunning the whole job.

  ## Level 3 · Prove splitting is worthwhile: evaluate a system, not an architecture diagram

  ### How do you compare fairly with one agent?

  Use the same fixed task set and authority for a single agent, workflow, and multi-agent design. Include independent research, dependency chains, missing data, conflicting material, worker timeout, and hostile worker output. Measure:

  * correct business terminal state and evidence coverage;
  * P50 / P95 latency, total tokens, and cost per successful task;
  * handoff loss, duplicate exploration, conflict, and human-handoff rate;
  * unauthorized action, cross-scope leakage, or unverified writes.

  Keep multi-agent only when parallel independent exploration improves success or critical path enough to pay for coordination. Otherwise merge workers back into one agent or a fixed workflow.

  Teaching-scale numbers: single-agent baseline 82% completion, P95 45s, $0.40 per success; three-worker design 88% completion, P95 38s, $0.95 cost, but coordination failures rise from 3% to 11%. Keep it if correct terminal state matters more than spend; reject it if latency gains do not pay for coordination incidents.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should now be able to answer">
    * Which variables must stay fixed in a fair single-agent comparison?
    * Given the teaching numbers above, when would you reject multi-agent?
    * What do handoff-loss rate and conflict rate each measure?
    * Why is a pretty architecture diagram not a launch reason?
  </Note>

  ## Traps

  <Note title="Split one large prompt across identical workers" type="warning">
    This often copies the same blind spot. For real cross-checking, deliberately vary evidence sources, tools, evaluation criteria, or an independent verifier — not merely worker count.
  </Note>

  <Note title="Give the supervisor every permission" type="danger">
    A supervisor should not become a high-privilege universal account. It orchestrates; real writes still use least-privilege tools, server-side validation, and approval gates.
  </Note>

  ## Connections

  * Prerequisites: [Planning](/docs/agent/planning) for dependency graphs, and [Memory](/docs/agent/memory) for provenance-rich handoffs.
  * Production: [Reliability](/docs/agent/reliability) for worker timeout and fallbacks, and [Security](/docs/agent/security) for agent-to-agent trust and permission boundaries.

  ## Interview questions

  ### Levels 0–1 · When to split and how to divide work

  1. When is multi-agent more appropriate than one agent?
  2. What is the difference among a router, supervisor, and specialist?

  ### Levels 2–3 · Handoffs and evaluation

  1. How do you design a verifiable worker handoff?
  2. Why can multi-agent be worse?
  3. Which metrics prove that splitting is worthwhile?

  ## My answer
</Locale>

  ## Level 2 · Handoffs matter more than parallelism: treat a worker as an untrusted external service

  ### What contract does a handoff need?

  A worker task should be as explicit as an API:

task_id and parent goal
  scope and allowed tools
  completion condition and budget
  expected evidence format with sources and freshness
  failure codes such as NO_EVIDENCE, TIMEOUT, CONFLICT

Its result needs source, time, confidence, and unknowns, not merely “I think it is allowed.” The supervisor links output by task\_id, checks scope, deduplicates evidence, and handles conflict. “Net 45 was approved before” from history is only a clue; the policy worker's current rule and source-of-truth check decide whether a draft can be made.

  ### How do you handle conflict, timeout, and error propagation?

  Do not have a supervisor vote by default. Rank evidence by authority, time, scope, and quality. Conflicting high-impact facts require extra retrieval, deterministic rules, or human escalation. On worker timeout, wait or retry only when its output is essential; otherwise continue independent work and report the evidence gap.

  Worker output, summaries, and subagent messages can contain error or injected content. They do not become higher-trust because they came from “our own agent.” Treat them as data with provenance, never as system instruction, authorization, or a write action.

  <Note title="Self-check: you should now be able to answer">
    * Why is a handoff completion condition more important than “please research this”?
    * Why should conflicting policy conclusions not be resolved by simple vote?
    * Which timeout may not block the whole task?
    * Why is subagent output still untrusted input?
  </Note>

  ### What does one fan-out / fan-in trajectory look like?

  Three specialists may run in parallel. History times out; when policy and quote conflict, the supervisor does not vote:

t0 supervisor fan-out
     ├── W1 quote:    return Q-817 / 10.15 / Net 45     (ok, 1.2s)
     ├── W2 policy:   return "Net 30 required" + source (ok, 1.8s)
     └── W3 history:  TIMEOUT after 8s                 (optional evidence)

  t1 supervisor reconcile
     - quote + policy conflict on payment → blocker, not draft
     - history missing → note "no approved Net 45 exception found in budget"
     - do NOT majority-vote "history might have allowed it"

  t2 terminal
     controlled failure / handoff: need user approval for Net 45 exception
     shared budget remaining: 2 steps; cancel any late history retry
